title: Ὄνοι πρὸς τὸν Δία
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 262. Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὄνοι ποτὲ ἀχθόμενοι ἐπὶ τῷ συνεχῶς ἀχθοφορεῖν καὶ ταλαιπωρεῖν πρέσβεις ἔπεμψαν πρὸς τὸν Δία, λύσιν τινὰ αἰτούμενοι τῶν πόνων.
sentences.tr: Onoi pote achthomenoi epi tōi synechōs achthophorein kai talaipōrein presbeis epempsan pros ton Dia, lysin tina aitoumenoi tōn ponōn.
sentences.l: Donkeys once, being vexed at their continually carrying burdens and suffering hardship, sent ambassadors to Zeus, asking for some release from their toils.
sentences.n: ἐπὶ τῷ … ἀχθοφορεῖν is an articular infinitive after ἐπί, 'at the carrying-of-burdens'. ἄχθομαι and ἀχθοφορέω come of the same root ἄχθος, a weight: they are weighed down at being made to bear weight. αἰτέομαι in the middle is to ask for a thing for oneself.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ αὐτοῖς ἐπιδεῖξαι βουλόμενος ὅτι τοῦτο ἀδύνατόν ἐστιν, ἔφη τότε αὐτοὺς ἀπαλλαγήσεσθαι τῆς κακοπαθείας, ὅταν οὐροῦντες ποταμὸν ποιήσωσι.
sentences.tr: Ho de autois epideixai boulomenos hoti touto adynaton estin, ephē tote autous apallagēsesthai tēs kakopatheias, hotan ourountes potamon poiēsōsi.
sentences.l: But he, wishing to show them that this is impossible, said that they would then be freed from their hardship, whenever by urinating they should make a river.
sentences.i: But Zeus, wanting to show them that the thing could not be, said they would be rid of their suffering on the day their urine made a river.
sentences.n: ἀπαλλάσσομαι takes the genitive of what one is rid of. ὅταν with the subjunctive ποιήσωσι sets a condition with no date to it, which is Zeus's whole point: the release is promised for a day that will not come.

sentences.t: Κἀκεῖνοι αὐτὸν ἀληθεύειν ὑπολαβόντες ἀπ’ ἐκείνου καὶ μέχρι νῦν ἔνθα ἂν ἀλλήλων οὖρον ἴδωσιν, ἐνταῦθα καὶ αὐτοὶ περιιστάμενοι οὐροῦσιν.
sentences.tr: Kakeinoi auton alētheuein hypolabontes ap’ ekeinou kai mechri nyn entha an allēlōn ouron idōsin, entautha kai autoi periistamenoi ourousin.
sentences.l: And they, having taken it that he was speaking truly, from that time and until now, wherever they see one another's urine, there they too, standing round about, urinate.
sentences.n: ἔνθα ἄν with the subjunctive is the indefinite relative, 'wherever it may be', answered by ἐνταῦθα. ἀπ’ ἐκείνου, 'from that time', with the present οὐροῦσιν brings the fable up to the reader's own day: it is told to account for a habit anyone may watch in the road.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι τὸ ἑκάστῳ πεπρωμένον ἀθεράπευτόν ἐστι.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti to hekastōi peprōmenon atherapeuton esti.
sentences.l: The story shows that what is fated for each is beyond remedy.
sentences.n: πεπρωμένον is a perfect passive participle used as a noun, 'the thing allotted' — fate as a portion measured out, with ἑκάστῳ the dative of the one it falls to. ἀθεράπευτος is what cannot be tended or treated.
